items.title: US Fed keen on the need to increase policy rates | The Manila Times
items.excerpt: November 15, 2026 SAN FRANCISCO Federal Reserve President Mary Daly said on Friday that her "bias" is that the central bank will need to increase its policy rate, particularly with services inflation moving in the wrong direction and some signs of inflation persistence. "We're going to need to, in all likelihood, raise rates; I will deliberate this with my colleagues in December at our meeting and in all future meetings and make the collective decision that we judge is most appropriate for the economy that is evolving," Daly said at a University of Nevada, Las Vegas Center for Business and Economic Research forecast event. "Producers are telling us more and more that they're running out of room to take it out of margins, and they really want to consider passing along this to consumers. So that's the inflationary impulse we want to avoid." The core consumer price index, which excludes volatile food and energy prices, has risen about 0.3 percent month over month in each of the last three months. That's far higher than the 0.2 percent or less that would be consistent with year-over-year inflation at 2 percent, the Fed's target. Daly, like several other policymakers, said she's particularly concerned that services inflation excluding housing is "not moving in the correct direction," which is particularly troubling because that slice of inflation tends to be sticky. "That's a place where you might think a retailer, or a professional business, if they have to buy more expensive IT goods, pay higher energy bills and have other inputs that are rising in price, maybe they're going to pass that along to customers," she said. The Fed raised its policy rate in September but held it steady in October, and financial markets are betting heavily on quarter-point interest-rate hikes at each of the Fed's December 8-9 and January 26-27 meetings. Daly said she feels markets understand how the Fed sets rates in response to economic conditions, without remarking specifically on the timing of coming rate hikes. Daly said she is also paying close attention to consumer spending, which accounts for most of the US economy, as the December meeting approaches. "Consumer spending remains just surprisingly resilient; you just haven't seen a pullback, so I think that's the piece of information that I'm really looking for in the next one to two to three months: what happens in that, especially around the holiday season, do we see consumers giving up or do we see them keeping going even if prices rise?" Daly said. "Sitting here in Las Vegas...we're just starting to hear that the consumer may be running out of gas. And we're hearing that now in other states, not just Nevada."

items.title: US consumer prices increase strongly for third straight month - Business Recorder
items.excerpt: WASHINGTON: US consumer prices increased more than expected in October, driven by higher costs for food and accommodation, leaving the Federal Reserve on course to raise interest rates next month. The Consumer Price Index report from the Labor Department on Tuesday also showed a strong buildup of underlying inflation pressures for the third straight month. The Labor Department’s Bureau of Labour Statistics did not publish year-over-year inflation readings because last year’s federal government shutdown prevented the collection of consumer price data in October 2025, leaving no comparison base. Annual consumer inflation jumped 3.7 percent in September. Inflation is running well above the US central bank’s 2 percent target. The US-Israeli war with Iran has boosted oil prices, combining with the import tariffs implemented by the Trump administration last year to lift the cost of living. High inflation contributed to the heavy losses suffered by President Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the midterm elections last week. Fed Governor Christopher Waller said on Tuesday that the US central bank should raise rates next month, adding that “a stronger policy move may be needed.” Waller also raised the prospect of a 50 basis point hike if core consumer prices, excluding food and energy, increased 0.3 percent or more from September, which they did. “Consumers’ inflation nightmare continues with no relief in sight,” said Christopher Rupkey, chief economist at FWDBONDS. “Fed officials are going to need to bring a bigger hose if they have any hope of putting the inflation fire out.” The CPI increased 0.4 percent last month after advancing 0.6 percent in September. It was the third consecutive month of CPI gains of 0.4 percent or more. Economists polled by Reuters had forecast the CPI climbing 0.3 percent over the month. Shelter, which includes rents, hotel and motel rooms, accounted for more than 30 percent of the increase in the CPI last month. Shelter costs rose 0.3 percent after climbing 0.4 percent in September. Food prices surged 0.5 percent after barely rising in the prior three months. Grocery store prices rebounded 0.4 percent, boosted by a 0.9 percent jump in the cost of beef. Egg prices rose 0.6 percent while fruits and vegetables were 0.6 percent more expensive. Prices for dairy and related products rose 0.6 percent. The cost of snacks surged 1.0 percent. Higher prices at the supermarket could be a reflection of more expensive diesel fuel. The cost of eating out also increased last month, with prices of food away from home surging 0.5 percent after rising 0.2 percent in September. The cost of full service meals increased 0.7 percent. Gasoline prices climbed 1.0 percent after soaring 9.1 percent. Though diesel prices have come down from record highs, they rose 2.7 percent last month after increasing 11.9 percent in September. STRONG CORE INFLATION Excluding the volatile food and energy components, the CPI increased 0.3 percent in October, advancing by the same margin for three months in a row. The so-called core CPI was forecast to have climbed 0.2 percent in October. Core CPI inflation increased 2.6 percent year-over-year in September. It was last month driven by a 0.3 percent rise in owners’ equivalent rent, a measure of the amount homeowners would pay to rent or would earn from renting their property.

items.title: How the Democrats’ midterm victory could reshape the rules for electing a US president | U.S. | EL PAÍS English
items.excerpt: Iker Seisdedos Javier Figueroa Washington / Miami - Nov 15, 2026 - 05:00 CET The Democrats’ historic victory at the November 3 midterm election promises to usher in a new era in Washington. It also opens the door to ending an electoral anomaly: the fact that the United States is the only presidential democracy in the world where the president is not elected directly by voters, but by an Electoral College. Here’s how it works: the Constitution assigns each of the 50 states a number of electors equal to its representation in Congress, two senators per state plus a number of members of the House of Representatives based on population, ranging from one to 52. With the exception of Maine and Nebraska, the candidate who wins a state receives all of its electoral votes, whether the margin is a single ballot or two million. Because Democrats won control of the governorship and both chambers of the state legislatures in Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Arizona and Nevada on November 3, advocates of this far-reaching reform now see a path to securing the support they previously lacked. Their strategy is to pass the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact, a legal framework first proposed in 2007 as an alternative to a constitutional amendment, which would be nearly impossible to achieve in a country as politically polarized as the United States. The compact has already been approved by 18 states and the District of Columbia, home to Washington. To take effect, it must be adopted by states representing a combined 270 electoral votes, the same number required to win the presidency. So far, states accounting for 222 electoral votes have joined. If Arizona, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and Nevada, the five states that have just turned blue, were to sign on, their combined 61 electoral votes would be enough to put the compact into force. ## Critics and supporters The Electoral College has many critics as well as supporters, who see it as a crucial component of the system of checks and balances designed by the Founding Fathers. The reality is that when they laid the foundations of the American republic, they could not have foreseen the central role political parties would come to play, since they did not yet exist, nor the extent to which the system would evolve into a rigid two-party structure. The current system allows a president to be elected without winning the popular vote. Both George W. Bush and Donald Trump reached the White House despite receiving fewer votes nationwide than their opponents, Al Gore and Hillary Clinton, in the 2000 and 2016 elections. Combined with the overrepresentation of less populous states, the Electoral College tends to favor Republicans, whose support is concentrated in states that wield disproportionate influence relative to their share of the national popular vote. This is one reason why presidential elections increasingly appear to be decided in advance, with only a handful of states truly in play. In 2024, there were seven such battleground states, and Trump carried every one of them: Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin, Nevada and North Carolina. If enacted, the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact could face legal challenges on the grounds that it may violate the Constitution’s Compact Clause. Found in Article I, Section 10, the clause provides that no state may enter into an agreement or compact with another state, or with a foreign power, without the consent of Congress. This route to changing the Electoral College system is easier than pursuing a constitutional amendment, but it is also more fragile. Just as states can join the compact, they can also withdraw from it, for example, if Republicans regain control of state government. Nor is it a given that demographic trends will always favor Democrats. Population shifts in recent years have cost traditionally blue states residents while boosting the populations of red states.

items.title: After midterm sweep, US Democrats split over Trump, cost-cutting agenda | The Straits Times
items.excerpt: Published Nov 15, 2026, 12:34 AM Updated Nov 15, 2026, 11:49 AM DENVER, Colorado – Fresh from a midterm election landslide, Democrats met in Denver this week, united in wanting to deliver voters relief from high costs, but split over how to achieve that, what lessons to draw from their victory, and how combative they should be towards President Donald Trump. Despite the celebratory mood after the Nov 3 rout of Republicans, tensions between moderates and a restive progressive wing surfaced at the party’s first major gathering since its victory, along with anxiety that the party could squander the opportunity voters had handed it. The gathering offered an early glimpse of the battle to define its future as prospective 2028 presidential candidates and senior leaders debated how to turn electoral success into a governing agenda while navigating longstanding ideological and generational divides. The conference, hosted by Majority Democrats, a group that advocates for younger party leaders and against left-wing activism, offered a forum for the jockeying now under way as Democrats debate what lessons to draw from their midterm win and begin the search for a 2028 White House standard-bearer. Speakers disagreed over whether to embrace a bolder progressive agenda or tack towards the centre, exposing competing approaches to lowering food, healthcare and housing costs, while working alongside Trump, who retains veto power for two more years. California Representative Ro Khanna, a progressive and potential presidential candidate, urged Democrats to stop chasing the political centre and embrace a bolder agenda, including universal healthcare, a wealth tax, a US$25 (S$32) federal minimum wage, deep Pentagon cuts and abolishing US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. By contrast, Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, a moderate and another potential 2028 contender, argued that the party should move beyond ideological litmus tests, saying voters “don’t give a damn” about such debates and care instead about whether Democrats can deliver results. The breadth of the Democratic victories has allowed moderates and progressives to argue that voters have endorsed their vision for the party’s future. “It’s to be expected that there will be a big debate because the Democratic victory was so broad, it swept in centrists, southern Democrats and more progressive and left-wing Democrats,” Democratic strategist Elaine Kamarck told Reuters. Trump retains significant executive authority to block much of the Democrats’ agenda, complicating the party’s efforts to lower costs – the central issue voters gave Democrats control of Congress to fix. Democrats are projected to hold at least 255 seats to the Republicans’ 169 in the US House, with 12 contests still undecided. In the Senate, the breakdown will be at least 55-44, with Democrats possibly gaining one more seat in Alaska when vote-counting is completed. ## Work with Trump or fight him? One of the most striking debates in Denver centred on how to govern with Trump still in the White House. James Talarico, the first Democrat elected to the US Senate from Texas since 1988, urged Democrats to work with Trump. “We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any presidency in American history,” Talarico said, drawing tepid applause. “We’re tired of being pitted against each other.” He found an ally in Iowa Governor-elect Rob Sand, who said he encouraged Democrats at campaign events to applaud Republicans and that partisan warfare will not deliver results. “The only way we’re going to fix that is by fixing it together,” Sand said. Minutes later, US Representative Jamie Raskin of Maryland and Eric Holder, who was attorney-general in the Obama administration, largely rejected accommodation with Trump. Raskin, expected to become chairman of the House Judiciary Committee in January and to oversee investigations into Trump in 2027, said the Republican Party had become an authoritarian cult of personality. “We’re going to reassert all of the powers of Congress that have been surrendered and abdicated by the MAGA Congress to King Trump,” Raskin said. “We’re going to enforce the Constitution against him.” Holder warned Democrats against pursuing bipartisanship. “If we retreat into caution, if we operate out of fear, if we take refuge in the niceties of the old Washington and seek approval from those who have been and are actively dismantling our institutions, we will fail.” There has been a long-simmering debate inside the party over whether to move farther left or pursue a more centrist agenda, and this election has only intensified those tensions. ## Competing visions for governing Almost everyone who spoke at the conference agreed that the party’s top priority was lowering costs and improving life for working families. It was a theme echoed by New York Representative Hakeem Jeffries, set to become US House Speaker, and several prospective 2028 presidential candidates, including Shapiro, Khanna and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg. But splits emerged over how to achieve that. Jeffries, a moderate, was heckled by a group of protesters, who accused him of being too timid to deliver change and called for a House leader who embraced a more populist progressive agenda. Khanna and Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, another progressive who this week challenged more centrist Senator Chuck Schumer of New York for the party’s top leadership job in the Senate, called for populist, government-funded economic solutions. ... There was a collective anxiety among the speakers that the party might squander one of the biggest victories it has achieved in a generation. Many speakers described the win not as an enduring mandate, but rather, a temporary opportunity voters had given them to fix the country’s problems.
